title: Contested
passages:
Pell's cradle rig coughed to life, the empty pod riding its locking pins like a coffin on a stretcher. He didn't look back at the shop door. The north gate's barrier arm rose on his warrant-token's last gasp, and the rig rolled out onto the haul road with its running lights cut, only the amber strobe on the cab roof pulsing slow against the pre-dawn dust.

Teodoro stood in the doorway, the dispatch handset warm against his ear. The board behind him had already begun to rewrite itself — resupply slots graying out one by one, the shift queue's count dropping as the line's trust score for Anza fell from green to amber to a flat, unblinking red.

"Resupply re-keys slow," he said into the handset, reading the board like a eulogy. "Diesel allocation recalculating. Food and filter carts pushed to next window. Shift queue starting to thin — names flagging for transfer review before the roster even posts." He paused, watching the winter diesel line go amber on the secondary display. "And now the winter diesel line's amber again. Whole new reason. The line doesn't like nodes that harbor witnesses."

Inside the shop, Rhea wiped grease from her knuckles and didn't look up. Ivo's cartridge hissed steady at his bedside, the counter climbing past twelve hours. Marlowe stood near the tool rack, his good hand cradling the other arm, watching the board change color.

Nour stood at the board, her tally card still in her jacket. She'd argued for handing him over. Kept her head down. Called it wisdom.

Doan hadn't moved from the ore stub. Wrist still looped in the locker cord. The overlap key hung from their belt, untouched.

Miko leaned against the tool rack, three coast tickets folded in her coat pocket.

The haul road swallowed Pell's rig whole. The strobe faded to a heartbeat in the dust, then nothing.

Teodoro set the handset down. "Board's frozen on our end too. No outgoing manifests until the contest clears. Which means no incoming resupply until the line decides we're not a liability."

"How long?" Rhea asked. Her voice was flat.

Teodoro shrugged. "Could be a shift. Could be a season. The line doesn't forget, and it doesn't hurry."

The winter diesel line pulsed amber. The shift queue kept thinning. And somewhere down the haul road, a cradle rig carried an empty pod north toward a line that had just learned Anza would bleed before it broke.

The board did what boards do when a node stops earning its keep. It started dropping names.

"That's the shift line," Teodoro said, before anyone asked, because Teodoro never waited to be asked. He tapped the column of names, each one a loader the line had cleared to work a shift at Anza. "Clearance comes down from the line, not up from us. Trust score goes red, clearances get pulled. Watch Ferris."

They watched Ferris. The name grayed, thinned to a hyphen, and then the row was empty except for a reason code nobody had to read aloud. NODE CONTESTED. CLEARANCE WITHDRAWN.

"Ojo," Teodoro said.

Ojo was standing right there with a load bar across his shoulders, waiting on a pallet that wasn't going to get scanned in. "That's me?"

"That's you."

"So I'm off."

"You're off the *board*. Different thing. Off the board you can't be paid, can't draw stores, and can't be relieved, because relief is a thing that only exists on boards." Teodoro spread his hands. "Congratulations. You're free."

"Free people eat," Ojo said. He set the load bar down on the deck, gently, like it might be listening.

"Free people eat somewhere else."

The Bautista row went next, both of them at once, and then four more nobody in the shop could have named without checking, and the shift line stopped being a list and started being an absence with a header on it.

Rhea did her own arithmetic out loud, the way she did everything. "Four cartridges in the drawer. One on Ivo. Resupply's pushed to a window Teodoro won't put a month on." She wiped her hands on a rag that was past helping. "So somebody tell me what the pallet's got to cover."

"Filters, water, and the diesel we already drew," Teodoro said. "In that order of optimism."

Nour hadn't moved from the board since Pell's strobe went out. She took the tally card out of her jacket — the paper count of seals drawn against seals actually hanging in the locker — and held it where the light could get at it.

"Eleven," she said. "Eleven seals short across four down-line runs. That's what I signed. The line sent back two filter carts and a diesel window in Ninth month, and I called that a good winter, and I called keeping my head down wisdom, and I was the one who stood here and told you the stranger in the box was worth less than the schedule." She turned the card over, then back. "The node's paying for the choice I lost. Not the one I made. The one I talked you out of. Hand him over, roster stays fat, everybody eats. That plan is dead on the deck and Anza is going to work doubles on half a pallet until the line cools off, and it will not hurry."

"Want a medal or a mop?" Miko said from the tool rack.

"I want it said out loud once, so it isn't only in my mouth."

"You want to cry, cry after the roster posts," Rhea said.

"I don't cry, I audit." Nour put the tally card down on the board ledge, face out, where anyone walking in could read her handwriting. "That stays there."

Doan's voice came from the ore stub, flat down the length of the shop. "That's evidence, Nour."

"It's a receipt."

The 06:00 bell went. Out on the floor, the overlap — the half hour where one shift hands the deck to the next and both are supposed to be standing on it — came and went with only one shift on it. The board filled in the relief slot without being asked. NO RELIEF POSTED. Then it did the same to Nour's line. NO RELIEF POSTED. Both rows re-keyed, doubled, and printed no end time.

Ospina watched the chipped die sitting in their palm and said, "At Kettering they'd have the roster back up inside the hour. With somebody else's names on it."

"Nobody's coming through that door," Doan said. Their wrist was still looped in the locker cord. "Great. I love overtime."

Nour hung her jacket on the board chair and sat down in it.

PASSAGE END

Teodoro turned from the board like a man turning from a fire he couldn't put out, and looked at Marlowe as if he'd only just filed him into the room.

"You're on the plate," he said. "Living crew, countersigned, the whole absurd business. Which means if you pass out on my deck I've got a body to explain, and a body is worse than weight." He jerked his chin at the cot in the back corner, the relay bunk where operators slept between line calls because the board never closed. "That's yours now. Relay keeps a bunk for whoever's holding the handset. Tonight that's me, so tonight it's yours. Sit down before you fall down."

"It's a shoulder," Marlowe said. "I've had worse loaded on me."

"Sure. And I've had worse told to me." Teodoro was already digging in the wall cabinet where the relay kept its splint kit — a real one, aluminum stays and a canvas sleeve, because relay techs climb the mast and cable tension breaks collarbones the same as a cargo strap does. "Arm out. Palm up. If you flinch I'll take it as a confession."

Marlowe gave him the arm. Teodoro worked the sleeve under it, thumbed the stay to length, and cinched the strap with the particular violence of a man who has done this before and resents every second.

"Too tight."

"It's supposed to be tight. Tight holds. Loose is a suggestion." He snugged it another notch, and Marlowe made a sound, and Teodoro nodded like the sound was data. "There. Now it's a shoulder instead of a rumor."

Rhea, from Ivo's bedside, without looking up: "He talks like this to the masts too."

"The masts don't sass back," Teodoro said. "You'd know that if you climbed anything but a tow hitch."

Marlowe lowered himself onto the bunk, slow, and the frame took his weight with a groan, and something in his face let go a little — the first time, maybe, he'd sat somewhere that was going to keep being there in the morning.

Across the shop, Ospina turned the chipped die over in their palm, catching the light on its broken corner. They'd been quiet since the countersign, watching the board shed names.

"This is the part that bites," they said, to no one, to everyone. They held the die up between two fingers. "This didn't countersign him. I never put this on the plate. It's the thing the Bay 4 hand used and dropped in the tool void — its corner matches the ballast plate because it's from the same batch, and that's all it ever was to me. Evidence. I carry it because a chipped die in the wrong pocket is a confession." They set it on the bench, gentle. "What countersigned him was me. My own seal authority, live, put on the plate by hand. And the second I put it there, it flagged. The review didn't file at Anza — it went up-line and it's sitting on Kettering's desk now."

"So there's a clock," Rhea said.

"A seal authority's only real while the desk says it's real," Ospina said. "Somebody at Kettering gets their coffee and my review to sign. If they sign it the wrong way, my authority's void, and a void countersign means Marlowe goes back to being weight. With better paperwork."

"So we've got till Kettering wakes up," Rhea said.

"We've got till Kettering *reads*," Ospina said.

Teodoro, who told you everything before you thought to ask: "The Kettering morning desk opens at 08:00 their time. A hundred and ten minutes from now." He said it the way other men say the weather.

Marlowe lay back against the relay wall, splinted arm across his chest, and looked at the ceiling like it owed him something. "Comfortable bunk. Great view of the thing that's going to unmake me."

"Free node, free view," Ojo said, from the deck, still not on the board.

Miko hadn't moved from the tool rack, but she wasn't leaning on it anymore. She'd gone still, the way she got before she did something stupid, three coast tickets a flat weight in her coat. Her eyes were on the ore stub. On Doan's back. On the wrist still looped in the locker cord.

The winter diesel line pulsed amber. A hundred and ten minutes.

Miko pushed off the rack.

The overlap locker was a gray steel cabinet at the mouth of the ore stub, tall as a door, and it held exactly one thing worth locking: the shift key, brass, on a retractable cord, worn by whoever was posted relief, so no shift could start work until the last one was standing there to hand it over.

Doan got there first. Not fast. Just first, the way you get to a thing you've been leaning on for six hours.

"Don't," they said.

"I haven't done anything yet."

"You've got the face. You get a face and then a thing happens."

"Open the locker."

"Take the key. Take the wrist with it, it's attached, I've stopped needing it."

Miko reached past them and worked the door pocket with two fingers. "Nobody locks the log," she said. "The overlap log — the paper both shifts sign in the thirty minutes we're all supposed to be on the deck at once. Handoff count, seal draw, who relieved who. You leave it in the pocket because locking it would be admitting somebody lies in it."

She came out with a folded sheaf of flimsy, soft at the creases from being opened and shut a thousand times.

"That's node paper," Doan said. "That's Nour's."

"Nour put her card face out on the ledge. She's in a confessing mood. Get in line."

Ospina crossed the shop, still turning the chipped die in their palm, and looked down at the page over Miko's shoulder. "Down-line seal runs," they said. "Anza draws seals from its own locker, crimps them on cargo going out, and the far bay signs for the count. That's a receiving line." They put a fingernail under one. "Bay, shift, count, hand mark."

Eleven lines had a hole where a count should be. Four runs. And every one of the four receiving lines carried the same bay, the same shift, and the same mark: three strokes and a bar through them.

"Bay 4, Shift 2," Ospina said. "That's a receiving mark, not a signature. The bay takes the stamp. Names live on the bay's own sheet at Kettering, and Kettering is a hundred and ninety kilometers up the haul road behind a reclaimer's strobe."

"So we've got the hand and not the man," Rhea said from Ivo's bedside. The cartridge hissed. The counter said 00:39.

"We've got the hand's *habit*," Ospina said. "Eleven short seals, one hand taking them in. That's not a shortage, that's a route."

Miko turned the page around and held it up. The Anza side of all eleven lines was filled in the same square, patient handwriting.

"That's yours," she said. "Eleven times."

"I write what's in front of me."

"Then write what's in front of you now."

Doan's jaw worked. "You say that name out loud in this shop and Pell's hands claim gets a name it can serve. That's not a witness. That's a delivery, with a bow on it. He's still out there with a live claim and an empty pod and nothing to put in it."

"So you'd rather he took one of us?"

"He'd rather take the one who's already been in a box," Doan said. "That's how reclamation works. It doesn't invent, it repeats."

"That's almost wisdom," Nour said from the board chair, without heat. "I don't recommend it. I did it for a year and look at the winter diesel line."

"You want to know what my crime is?" Doan said. "I carried eleven seals down that stub and never asked what they were for. Asking costs. Not asking is free. Mine's already on the paper, it's not going on a board too."

Behind them, Teodoro hadn't stopped reading.

"Sena," he said.

The row grayed, thinned to a hyphen, and printed its reason code.

"Amaru, both. Pike." He tapped as he went, unhurried, a man calling a tide. "Nine clearances left on the line."

"Eight," he said, when the next one went.

Marlowe watched from the relay bunk with the splinted arm across his chest and said nothing at all, which for a man who'd been counted down into a lid was restraint.

Miko held the log open with her thumb, the way you hold a door against wind. "Say it while it's still worth something."

"It isn't worth anything. That's what makes it cheap."

The little light on the key fob in Doan's fist went out — dead metal now, brass and a cord and no authority in it anywhere. On the board, Doan's own row thinned to a hyphen and printed NODE CONTESTED. CLEARANCE WITHDRAWN.

"Seven," Teodoro said.

Doan laughed at the ceiling like it had finally told a decent joke.

Marlowe didn't sit up. Didn't turn his head. The words came from the bunk like smoke from a cracked manifold, flat and patient and aimed at the ceiling.

"The voice that counted me down," he said. "Three, two, one, lid. I knew it. I've signed cargo to that voice for two seasons. Bay 4, Shift 2. Far-end contact on the receiving sheet. The loader who tells me the count is clean and the seals match and the rig's good to roll." He swallowed, the sound loud in the sudden quiet. "The same voice that resealed the four rigs after I was inside. Stood there watching the lid come down. Counted me into the dark like I was a pallet of filters."

The shop didn't breathe.

Doan's laugh died in their throat. Their hand went slack on the dead key fob.

Nour didn't look up from the tally card on the ledge. Her fingers traced the edge of the paper, once, twice. Then she set her palm flat on the board chair's arm and said it, quiet as a shift bell.

"Calder."

The name hit the room like a dropped wrench.

"Calder Voss," Nour said. "Bay 4, Shift 2. Kettering. He's the one who takes the short seals. He's the one who counts the handovers. He's the one who told me the resupply window would hold if I didn't ask where the seals went." She finally looked up, and her face was the board — gray lines, red reason codes, no warmth left in any of it. "He's the forger. He's the hand. And he's the one Marlowe trusted to receive his cargo."

Ospina's die stopped turning in their fingers. "Calder Voss. Seal authority, Bay 4, Shift 2. Same shift as me. Same bay." They set the die down on the bench, deliberate. "His authority's clean. Always has been. That's how he got the stamps past the desk."

"Clean until somebody looks," Rhea said. She was standing now, at Ivo's bedside, the cartridge hissing behind her. "Which means Kettering's morning desk has a name to put to the review on your authority. And a name to put to the forger who's been running the Bay 4 side of this."

Miko folded the overlap log slow, precise, and tucked it into her coat alongside the three coast tickets. "So the man who boxed Marlowe is the man who receives at Kettering. The man who counted him down is the man who resealed the rigs. And the man Nour made the deal with is the man Pell's hands claim is still looking for a body to put in that pod."

"Calder Voss," Teodoro said, tapping it into the board's open note field like he was logging a filter change. "Bay 4, Shift 2. Far-end contact. Forger. Resealer. Hands claim active." He looked at the room. "Anyone want to tell me why a Kettering loader with clean authority and a resupply pipeline just happened to seal a living man into a ballast pod and ship him down the line?"

"Because the line doesn't ask," Doan said. Their voice was thin, stripped of the joke. "It only counts. And Calder makes the counts work."

"Seven clearances," Teodoro read from the board. "Six. Five."

The winter diesel line pulsed amber.

Out on the haul road, a hundred and ninety kilometers north, a service rig's running lights cut through the pre-dawn dust, and the chipped die in Ospina's pocket weighed more than the bunk Marlowe was lying on.
